diagram_classification: Cosmological / meteorological: a twelve-wind rose (wind wheel) with a human head at the centre, in the tradition of Isidore of Seville's De natura rerum and Etymologiae XIII.
interpretation: The diagram is a wind rose that divides the horizon into twelve sectors, each named for a wind, in the manner of the Isidorian system of twelve winds. Each sector carries a pair of names, in red and in black. The red names are Latin and the black ones are Greek or alternative names. The red names read EURUS, EURO AUSTER, AUSTER, AUSTRO AFRICUS, AFRICUS, FAVONIUS, CHORUS, CIRCIUS, SEPTENTRIO, AQUILO, VULTURNUS and SUBSOLANUS. The black names include eurus, euronotus, notus, libonotus, lips, zephyrus, argestes, thrascias, aparctias, boreas, caecias and apeliotes. The rose is oriented with east at the top, and the cardinal winds sit at the points marked with yellow triquetra knots. Subsolanus is the east wind, Auster the south, Favonius or Zephyrus the west, and Septentrio the north. The intermediate winds fill the spaces between them. The head at the centre most likely represents the human being, or the earth, as the microcosm that receives the winds. It may also be a personification of the wind-source or of the cosmos. The head fits the medieval conception of the world as a body and of man as a microcosm, but it is not explained by any label, so this reading is less secure than the identification of the winds. The wheel shows the structure of the winds as part of the order of nature, within a treatise on natural phenomena.
evidence: Visible: a circle divided by radii into twelve sectors, with a red Latin name and a black alternative name in each. Visible: eight triangular knot ornaments in yellow and blue-grey on the rim, and a central roundel with a profile human head. Textual: legible names such as EURUS, AUSTER, AFRICUS, FAVONIUS, CHORUS, CIRCIUS, SEPTENTRIO, AQUILO, VULTURNUS, SUBSOLANUS, plus the black names zephyrus, lips, notus, boreas and others, match the twelve-wind scheme. External: the layout recalls the Isidorian wind diagrams in De natura rerum, and the Insular-style knot ornaments suggest a manuscript of that tradition. The interpretation of the central head as microcosm or personified earth is inferred from medieval conventions, not from any inscription, so it carries lower certainty.
